claim: Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) are specialized sensory cells in the intestinal epithelium that sense and transduce nutrient information.
source: Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) are specialized sensory cells in the intestinal epithelium that sense and transduce nutrient information.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the function of EECs.

claim: High fat feeding alters EEC morphology.
source: Our results reveal that high fat feeding alters EEC morphology and converts them into a nutrient insensitive state that is coupled to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: High fat feeding converts EECs into a nutrient insensitive state.
source: Our results reveal that high fat feeding alters EEC morphology and converts them into a nutrient insensitive state that is coupled to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing reduced EEC calcium responses to nutrients after high fat feeding.

claim: High fat diet induced EEC changes are coupled to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
source: Our results reveal that high fat feeding alters EEC morphology and converts them into a nutrient insensitive state that is coupled to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data showing ER stress markers in EECs after high fat feeding.

claim: The novel adaptation of EECs to high fat feeding is called 'EEC silencing'.
source: We called this novel adaptation 'EEC silencing'.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors for the phenomenon they observed.

claim: Germ-free zebrafish are resistant to high fat diet induced EEC silencing.
source: Gnotobiotic studies revealed that germ-free zebrafish are resistant to high fat diet induced EEC silencing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gnotobiotic experiments comparing germ-free and conventionalized zebrafish.

claim: High fat feeding altered gut microbiota composition including enrichment of Acinetobacter bacteria.
source: High fat feeding altered gut microbiota composition including enrichment of Acinetobacter bacteria, and we identified an Acinetobacter strain sufficient to induce EEC silencing.
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data showing changes in microbial community composition.

claim: An Acinetobacter strain is sufficient to induce EEC silencing.
source: High fat feeding altered gut microbiota composition including enrichment of Acinetobacter bacteria, and we identified an Acinetobacter strain sufficient to induce EEC silencing.
evidence: This is supported by monoassociation experiments showing that Acinetobacter sp. ZOR0008 alone can induce EEC morphological changes during high fat feeding.

claim: The transcription factor NeuroD1 plays an essential role to restrict intestinal progenitor cells to an EEC fate in mice.
source: Previous mouse studies have shown that the transcription factor NeuroD1 plays an essential role to restrict intestinal progenitor cells to an EEC fate (Li et al., 2011; Ray and Leiter, 2007), and is expressed in almost all EECs without expression in other intestinal epithelial cell lineages (Li et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mouse studies.

claim: NeuroD1 is expressed in almost all EECs without expression in other intestinal epithelial cell lineages in mice.
source: Previous mouse studies have shown that the transcription factor NeuroD1 plays an essential role to restrict intestinal progenitor cells to an EEC fate (Li et al., 2011; Ray and Leiter, 2007), and is expressed in almost all EECs without expression in other intestinal epithelial cell lineages (Li et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mouse studies.

claim: Neurod1+ cells in the zebrafish intestine label cells that express the intestinal secretory cell marker 2F11.
source: We found that both lines labeled cells in the intestinal epithelium of 6 dpf zebrafish (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and that these neurod1+ cells do not overlap with goblet cells and express the intestinal secretory cell marker 2F11 (Crosnier et al., 2005) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Neurod1+ cells in the zebrafish intestine do not overlap with goblet cells.
source: We found that both lines labeled cells in the intestinal epithelium of 6 dpf zebrafish (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and that these neurod1+ cells do not overlap with goblet cells and express the intestinal secretory cell marker 2F11 (Crosnier et al., 2005) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing no overlap between neurod1+ cells and goblet cell markers.

claim: Neurod1+ cells in the zebrafish intestine do not overlap with tp1+ cells.
source: In accord, we found that neurod1+ cells in the intestine do not overlap with tp1+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data from double transgenic zebrafish.

claim: Activation of Notch signaling is essential to restrict intestinal progenitor cells to an absorptive cell fate.
source: Activation of Notch signaling is essential to restrict intestinal progenitor cells to an absorptive cell fate (Crosnier et al., 2005; Li et al., 2012), suggesting tp1+ cells may represent enterocyte progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neurod1+ cells in the zebrafish intestine do not overlap with the mature enterocyte marker ifabp/fabp2.
source: Additionally, our results demonstrated that neurod1+ cells in the intestine do not overlap with the mature enterocyte marker ifabp/fabp2 (Kanther et al., 2011) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: EECs in the zebrafish intestine are post-mitotic.
source: In addition, using EdU labeling in 5 dpf zebrafish larvae, we found that EECs in the intestine are post-mitotic and require about 30 hr to differentiate from proliferating progenitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EdU tracing experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: EECs in the zebrafish intestine require about 30 hr to differentiate from proliferating progenitors.
source: In addition, using EdU labeling in 5 dpf zebrafish larvae, we found that EECs in the intestine are post-mitotic and require about 30 hr to differentiate from proliferating progenitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EdU tracing experiments showing the timing of EEC differentiation.

claim: PYY and CCK hormones are only expressed in EECs in the proximal intestine of zebrafish.
source: We found that PYY and CCK hormones, which are important for regulating fat digestion and feeding behavior, are only expressed in EECs in the proximal intestine where dietary fats and other nutrients are digested and absorbed (Carten et al., 2011; Farber et al., 2001) (Figure 1I–J).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 1I–J.

claim: PYY and CCK are important for regulating fat digestion and feeding behavior.
source: We found that PYY and CCK hormones, which are important for regulating fat digestion and feeding behavior, are only expressed in EECs in the proximal intestine where dietary fats and other nutrients are digested and absorbed (Carten et al., 2011; Farber et al., 2001) (Figure 1I–J).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Somatostatin expression occurs in EECs along the whole zebrafish intestine.
source: In contrast, somatostatin expression occurred in EECs along the whole intestine and glucagon expressing EECs were found along the proximal and mid-intestine (segment 2) but excluded from the posterior intestine (segment 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G.

claim: Glucagon expressing EECs are found along the proximal and mid-intestine but excluded from the posterior intestine in zebrafish.
source: In contrast, somatostatin expression occurred in EECs along the whole intestine and glucagon expressing EECs were found along the proximal and mid-intestine (segment 2) but excluded from the posterior intestine (segment 3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G.

claim: Transient increases in intracellular calcium concentration are an important mediator and indicator of EEC function.
source: Therefore, the transient increase in intracellular calcium concentration is an important mediator and indicator of EEC function.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EEC physiology.

claim: Palmitate activates a subset of EECs in zebrafish.
source: We found that palmitate, but not the BSA vehicle control, activated a subset of EECs (Figure 2B–F, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B–F and Video 1.

claim: Linoleate and dodecanoate induce EEC activity in zebrafish.
source: Similar patterns of EEC activation in the proximal intestine were induced by the fatty acids linoleate and dodecanoate; whereas, the short chain fatty acid butyrate did not induce EEC activity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The short chain fatty acid butyrate does not induce EEC activity in zebrafish.
source: Similar patterns of EEC activation in the proximal intestine were induced by the fatty acids linoleate and dodecanoate; whereas, the short chain fatty acid butyrate did not induce EEC activity (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ability of EECs to respond to palmitate stimulation is significantly reduced after 6 hr of high fat meal feeding.
source: To our surprise, we found that the ability of EECs in the proximal intestine to respond to palmitate stimulation in our EEC activity assay was quickly and significantly reduced after 6 hr of HF meal feeding (Figure 2H–J, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2H–J and Video 2.

claim: Glucose stimulation activates EECs only in the proximal intestine of zebrafish under unfed control conditions.
source: Similar to fatty acids, glucose stimulation activated EECs only in the proximal intestine of the zebrafish under unfed control conditions (Figure 3A and B, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Glucose-stimulated elevation of intracellular calcium concentrations and hormone secretion in EECs is dependent upon the EEC sodium dependent glucose cotransporter 1 (Sglt1) in mammals.
source: Previous mammalian cell culture studies reported that glucose-stimulated elevation of intracellular calcium concentrations and hormone secretion in EECs is dependent upon the EEC sodium dependent glucose cotransporter 1 (Sglt1), an apical membrane protein that is expressed in small intestine and renal tubules and actively transports glucose and galactose into cells (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous mammalian study.

claim: Sglt1 is expressed on the apical surface of zebrafish intestinal epithelial cells including enterocytes and EECs.
source: Similarly, we found that Sglt1 is expressed on the apical surface of zebrafish intestinal epithelial cells including enterocytes and EECs (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Co-stimulation with glucose and phlorizin, a chemical inhibitor of Sglt1, blocks EEC activation induced by glucose in zebrafish.
source: In addition, co-stimulation with glucose and phlorizin, a chemical inhibitor of Sglt1, blocked the EEC activation induced by glucose (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3F–G.

claim: The EEC response to glucose stimulation is significantly increased by the addition of NaCl in the stimulant solution in zebrafish.
source: Consistently, the EEC response to glucose stimulation was significantly increased by the addition of NaCl in the stimulant solution which will facilate sodium gradient dependent glucose transport by Sglt1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Zebrafish EECs respond to galactose but not fructose.
source: In addition, zebrafish EECs also responded to the other Sglt1 substrate, galactose, but not fructose (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: High fat feeding significantly reduces EECs' response to subsequent glucose stimulation in zebrafish.
source: Indeed, HF feeding significantly reduced EECs' response to subsequent glucose stimulation (Figure 3H–J, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3H–J and Video 3.

claim: Zebrafish EECs respond to cysteine stimulation primarily in the mid intestine.
source: However, in contrast to the fatty acid and glucose responses, zebrafish EECs that responded to cysteine were located primarily in the mid intestine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B) and HF meal ingestion did not significantly impair subsequent EEC responses to cysteine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: High fat meal ingestion does not significantly impair subsequent EEC responses to cysteine in zebrafish.
source: However, in contrast to the fatty acid and glucose responses, zebrafish EECs that responded to cysteine were located primarily in the mid intestine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B) and HF meal ingestion did not significantly impair subsequent EEC responses to cysteine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Most EECs in zebrafish under control conditions are in an open-type morphology with an apical process that extends to the intestinal lumen.
source: In zebrafish under control conditions, most EECs are in an open-type morphology (Figure 1B–G) with an apical process that extends to the intestinal lumen, allowing them to directly interact with the contents of the intestinal lumen (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 1B–G and 4A.

claim: Most EECs in the proximal zebrafish intestine adopt a closed-type morphology after 6 hr of high fat feeding.
source: When we examined the proximal zebrafish intestine after 6 hr of HF feeding, we discovered that most EECs had adopted a closed-type morphology that apparently lacked an apical extension and no longer had access to the lumenal contents (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The change in EEC morphology during high fat feeding is not due to EEC turnover.
source: However, we did not observe the presence of any green EECs following HF feeding (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F–G).
evidence: This is supported by photoconversion tracing experiments showing no newly generated EECs after HF feeding.

claim: High fat feeding does not induce EEC apoptosis.
source: However, we did not detect activation of apoptosis in closed-type EECs following HF diet feeding (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: High fat feeding does not significantly change EEC cell volume.
source: Consistently, we also did not observe a significant change in EEC cell volume following HF feeding (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by cell volume quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The EEC morphology score gradually decreases upon high fat feeding in zebrafish.
source: We found that the EEC morphology score gradually decreased upon HFfeeding (Figure 4E, Video 5), indicating that EECs had changed from an open-type to closed-type morphology.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4E and Video 5.

claim: EEC apical processes undergo dynamic retraction after high fat feeding in zebrafish.
source: Using in vivo confocal time-lapse imaging in Tg(neurod1:lifeAct-EGFP) zebrafish, we confirmed that EEC apical processes undergo dynamic retraction after HF feeding (Figure 4F), which was not observed in control animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C and D, Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4F and Video 6.

claim: EECs in the distal-intestine retain their open-type morphology following high fat feeding in zebrafish.
source: Interestingly, EECs in the distal-intestine retained their open-type morphology following HF feeding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H), suggesting the adaptation from open- to closed-type EEC morphology is a specific response of EECs in the proximal intestine.
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: High fat feeding triggers a similar open- to closed-type change in EEC morphology in adult zebrafish proximal intestine.
source: Our results demonstrated that, consistent with our observations in larvae zebrafish, 10 hr HF feeding triggered a similar open- to closed-type change in EEC morphology in adult zebrafish proximal intestine (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data from adult zebrafish shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: EECs' calcium response to palmitate parallels the clearance of the high fat meal from the intestine.
source: We observed that EECs' calcium response to palmitate paralleled the clearance of the HF meal from the intestine (Figure 5A,B and G).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data during recovery shown in Figure 5A, B, and G.

claim: Twenty hours after high fat feeding, the EEC calcium response to palmitate is restored comparable to that of unfed controls.
source: Twenty hours after HF feeding, intestinal fat was almost completely cleared from the intestine and the EEC calcium response to palmitate was restored comparable to that of unfed controls (Figure 5B and H).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5B and H.

claim: After 20 hr of recovery from high fat feeding, the apical extension of most EECs returns to the intestinal lumen and the EEC morphology score normalizes.
source: After 20 hr of recovery from HF feeding, the apical extension of most EECs had returned to the intestinal lumen and the EEC morphology score normalized (Figure 5C–F and I).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5C–F and I.

claim: High fat feeding does not induce EEC apoptosis during recovery.
source: Almost all EECs in the recovered zebrafish were labeled with red Kaede (Figure 5J–K) indicating that HF feeding did not induce EEC apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by Kaede tracing data shown in Figure 5J–K.

claim: EECs' morphological and functional adaptations in response to high fat feeding are transient and reversible.
source: In summary, our data suggest that EECs' morphological and functional adaptations in response to HF feeding are transient and reversible.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recovery experiments showing restoration of EEC function and morphology.

claim: High fat feeding increases expression of transcripts encoding EEC hormones in zebrafish digestive tracts.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR assays in dissected zebrafish digestive tracts 6 hr after HF feeding revealed broad increases in expression of transcripts encoding EEC hormones (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The largest increases in EEC hormone transcript expression after high fat feeding are pyyb and ccka.
source: The largest increases were pyyb and ccka (Figure 6A), both of which are expressed by EECs in the proximal zebrafish intestine (Figure 1) and are important for the response to dietary lipid.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: High fat feeding does not significantly alter expression of EEC specific transcription factors (neurod1, pax6b, isl1) in zebrafish.
source: However, HF feeding did not significantly alter expression of EEC specific transcription factors (neurod1, pax6b, isl1), nor the total number of EECs per animal (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and quantification data shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: High fat feeding does not significantly alter the total number of EECs per animal in zebrafish.
source: However, HF feeding did not significantly alter expression of EEC specific transcription factors (neurod1, pax6b, isl1), nor the total number of EECs per animal (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: High fat feeding leads to gradual increases in ccka and pyyb transcript levels which plateau 6 hr after high fat feeding.
source: We found that HF feeding led to gradual increases in ccka and pyyb transcript levelss which plateaued 6 hr after HF feeding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by time-course qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: PYY immunofluorescence reveals reduced fluorescence intensity at 5 hr and 8 hr post high fat fed zebrafish compared to control zebrafish.
source: Despite these increases in transcript level, PYY immunofluorescence revealed that reduced fluorescence intensity at 5 hr and 8 hr post HF fed zebrafish compared to control zebrafish (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D and F.

claim: High fat feeding increases expression of UPR genes including chaperone proteins Gpr94 and Bip as early as 2 hr after high fat feeding in zebrafish.
source: Using quantitative RT-PCR analysis in dissected zebrafish digestive tracts, we found that HF feeding increased expression of UPR genes including chaperone proteins Gpr94 and Bip as early as 2 hr after HF feeding (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: High fat feeding significantly induces GFP expression in neurod1+ EECs in Tg(ef1α:xbp1δ-gfp) zebrafish.
source: We crossed Tg(ef1α:xbp1δ-gfp) with Tg(neurod1:RFP) zebrafish and found that zebrafish larvae fed a HF meal, but not control larvae, displayed a significant induction of GFP in neurod1+ EECs (Figure 6L–N; Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6L–N and Videos 7 and 8.

claim: Treatment with TUDCA prevents high fat feeding induced reduction in EEC morphology score.
source: Whereas HF feeding normally reduces the EEC morphology score, this did not occur in zebrafish treated with tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), a known ER stress inhibitor (Uppala et al., 2017; Vang et al., 2014) (Figure 6O–Q).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6O–Q.

claim: Thapsigargin treatment reduces the EEC calcium response to both glucose and palmitate in zebrafish.
source: Thapsigargin treatment, however, reduced the EEC calcium response in that region to both glucose and palmitate (Figure 6D–I, Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–E) and decreased the EEC morphology score, both key phenomena associated with EEC silencing (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging and morphology data shown in Figure 6D–I, J, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–E.

claim: Treatment with brefeldin A (BFA) significantly decreases the EEC morphology score.
source: Similar to thapsigargin, treatment with BFA significantly decreased the EEC morphology score (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is supported by morphology quantification data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Treatment with orlistat during high fat feeding significantly increases the ability of EECs to subsequently respond to glucose and palmitate in zebrafish.
source: We found that treatment of Tg(neurod1:Gcamp6f) zebrafish with orlistat during HF feeding significantly increased the ability of EECs to subsequently respond to glucose and palmitate (Figure 7A–F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7A–F.

claim: Treatment with orlistat prevents high fat induced EEC morphological changes in zebrafish.
source: By contrast, treatment with orlistat prevented HF induced EEC morphological changes (Figure 7H and N), suggesting lipase activity is required for EEC silencing.
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7H and N.

claim: Orlistat treatment significantly reduces the percentage of EECs that are ef1α:xbp1δ-gfp+ following high fat feeding in zebrafish.
source: We found that orlistat treatment significantly reduced the percentage of EECs that are ef1α:xbp1δ-gfp+ following HF feeding (Figure 7I,J and O).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7I, J, and O.

claim: High fat feeding significantly increases the number of NF-κB+ EECs in zebrafish.
source: After crossing a transgenic reporter of NF-κB activity Tg(NFkB:EGFP) (Kanther et al., 2011) with Tg(neurod1:RFP), we found that HF feeding significantly increased the number of NF-κB+ EECs (Figure 7K and P), but that this effect could be significantly reduced by treatment with orlistat or the ER stress inhibitor TUDCA (Figure 7L,M and P).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7K and P.

claim: Treatment with orlistat or TUDCA significantly reduces high fat feeding induced increase in NF-κB+ EECs.
source: After crossing a transgenic reporter of NF-κB activity Tg(NFkB:EGFP) (Kanther et al., 2011) with Tg(neurod1:RFP), we found that HF feeding significantly increased the number of NF-κB+ EECs (Figure 7K and P), but that this effect could be significantly reduced by treatment with orlistat or the ER stress inhibitor TUDCA (Figure 7L,M and P).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7L, M, and P.

claim: Treatment with palmitate for 6 hr significantly reduces the ability of EECs to respond to subsequent palmitate stimulation in zebrafish.
source: Treatment with palmitate for 6 hr significantly reduced the ability of EECs to respond to subsequent palmitate stimulation, but did not influence the EEC morphology score, nor the EEC response toward subsequent glucose stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging and morphology data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: Palmitate treatment does not influence the EEC morphology score in zebrafish.
source: Treatment with palmitate for 6 hr significantly reduced the ability of EECs to respond to subsequent palmitate stimulation, but did not influence the EEC morphology score, nor the EEC response toward subsequent glucose stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by morphology quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: Palmitate treatment does not influence the EEC response toward subsequent glucose stimulation in zebrafish.
source: Treatment with palmitate for 6 hr significantly reduced the ability of EECs to respond to subsequent palmitate stimulation, but did not influence the EEC morphology score, nor the EEC response toward subsequent glucose stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: Palmitate treatment does not induce significant ER stress activation like high fat feeding in zebrafish.
source: Similary, using Tg(ef1α:xbp1δ-gfp) and real-time PCR to examine relative bip and grp94 expression, we found that palmitate treatment did not induce significant ER stress activation like HF feeding (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: There are no significant differences between germ-free and conventionalized zebrafish in their EEC morphology score or EEC response to palmitate in the absence of high fat feeding.
source: In the absence of HF feeding, we observed no significant differences between GF and CV zebrafish in their EEC morphology score or EEC response to palmitate (Figure 8C,D,G and I).
evidence: This is supported by morphology and calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8C, D, G, and I.

claim: EECs in germ-free zebrafish do not show a change in morphology after high fat feeding.
source: In contrast to CV HF-fed zebrafish larvae, EECs in GF zebrafish did not show a change in morphology after HF feeding (Figure 8A,B and I) and exhibited significantly greater responses to palmitate stimulation (Figure 8E,F and H).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 8A, B, and I.

claim: EECs in germ-free zebrafish exhibit significantly greater responses to palmitate stimulation after high fat feeding compared to conventionalized zebrafish.
source: In contrast to CV HF-fed zebrafish larvae, EECs in GF zebrafish did not show a change in morphology after HF feeding (Figure 8A,B and I) and exhibited significantly greater responses to palmitate stimulation (Figure 8E,F and H).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8E, F, and H.

claim: The ability of high fat feeding to induce reporters of ER stress and NF-κB activation is significantly reduced in germ-free compared to conventionalized zebrafish.
source: In accord, the ability of HF feeding to induce reporters of ER stress and NF-κB activation was significantly reduced in GF compared to CV zebrafish (Figure 8J and K).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 8J and K.

claim: EECs' response to palmitate after high fat feeding in myd88 mutant zebrafish is equivalent to that of wild type fish.
source: We found that EECs' response to palmitate after HF feeding was equivalent to that of wild type fish (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), suggesting microbiota promote EEC silencing in a Myd88-independent manner.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intestinal microbiota abundance increases approximately 20 fold following 6 hr of high fat feeding in zebrafish.
source: Strikingly, we found that intestinal microbiota abundance had increased ~20 fold following 6 hr of HF feeding (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by CFU analysis data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: High fat feeding has relatively large effects on overall bacterial community structure in both gut and media samples in zebrafish.
source: Analysis of bacterial community structure using the Weighted Unifrac method (Caporaso et al., 2010) revealed, as expected, relatively large differences between gut and media samples (PERMANOVA p<0.02 control gut vs. control media, p<0.005 HF gut vs HF media) (Figure 9C). The addition of HF feeding had a relatively smaller but consistent effect on overall bacterial community structure in both gut and media (PERMANOVA p=0.2 control gut vs HF gut, p=0.094 control media vs HF media) (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and PCoA analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: High fat feeding markedly decreases the relative abundance of members of class Betaproteobacteria in zebrafish media.
source: Members of class Betaproteobacteria dominated the control media, but HF feeding markedly decreased their relative abundance (LDA effect size 5.45, p=0.049).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and LEfSe analysis.

claim: High fat feeding increases the relative abundance of members of class Gammaproteobacteria in zebrafish media.
source: Conversely, HF feeding increased the relative abundance of members of class Gammaproteobacteria (LDA effect size 5.49, p=0.049; Figure 9D) such as genera Acinetobacter (LDA effect size 5.13, p=0.049), Pseudomonas (LDA effect size 5.02, p=0.049) and Aeromonas (LDA effect size 4.78, p=0.049; Figure 9F; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 9D and F.

claim: High fat feeding increases the relative abundance of genus Acinetobacter in zebrafish media.
source: Conversely, HF feeding increased the relative abundance of members of class Gammaproteobacteria (LDA effect size 5.49, p=0.049; Figure 9D) such as genera Acinetobacter (LDA effect size 5.13, p=0.049), Pseudomonas (LDA effect size 5.02, p=0.049) and Aeromonas (LDA effect size 4.78, p=0.049; Figure 9F; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: High fat feeding increases the relative abundance of genus Pseudomonas in zebrafish media.
source: Conversely, HF feeding increased the relative abundance of members of class Gammaproteobacteria (LDA effect size 5.49, p=0.049; Figure 9D) such as genera Acinetobacter (LDA effect size 5.13, p=0.049), Pseudomonas (LDA effect size 5.02, p=0.049) and Aeromonas (LDA effect size 4.78, p=0.049; Figure 9F; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: High fat feeding increases the relative abundance of genus Aeromonas in zebrafish media.
source: Conversely, HF feeding increased the relative abundance of members of class Gammaproteobacteria (LDA effect size 5.49, p=0.049; Figure 9D) such as genera Acinetobacter (LDA effect size 5.13, p=0.049), Pseudomonas (LDA effect size 5.02, p=0.049) and Aeromonas (LDA effect size 4.78, p=0.049; Figure 9F; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: High fat feeding increases the relative abundance of class Cytophagia in zebrafish media.
source: HF feeding also increased the relative abundance in media of class Cytophagia from phylum Bacteroidetes (LDA effect size 4.66, p=0.049; Figure 9D) due to increases in the genus Flectobacillus (LDA effect size 4.76, p=0.049; Figure 9E; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 9D and E.

claim: High fat feeding increases the relative abundance of genus Flectobacillus in zebrafish media.
source: HF feeding also increased the relative abundance in media of class Cytophagia from phylum Bacteroidetes (LDA effect size 4.66, p=0.049; Figure 9D) due to increases in the genus Flectobacillus (LDA effect size 4.76, p=0.049; Figure 9E; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claim: High fat feeding significantly increases abundance of class Cytophagia in zebrafish gut microbiotas.
source: However, similar to the media, HF feeding significantly increased abundance of class Cytophagia (LDA effect size 4.01, p=0.018; Figure 9D) due to enrichment of Flectobacillus (LDA effect size 4.01, p=0.004; Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 9D and F.

claim: High fat feeding results in a 100-fold increase in the relative abundance of Acinetobacter sp. in the zebrafish gut.
source: Additionally, HF feeding resulted in a 100-fold increase the relative abundance of Acinetobacter sp. in the gut (average 0.04% in control gut, 4.28% in HF gut; LDA effect size 4.31, p=0.001; Figure 9G, Supplementary file 2 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and LEfSe analysis shown in Figure 9G.

claim: Acinetobacter sp. ZOR0008 is sufficient to significantly reduce the EEC morphology score upon high fat feeding in monoassociated zebrafish.
source: Strikingly, only Acinetobacter sp. ZOR0008 was sufficient to significantly reduce the EEC morphology score upon HF feeding (Figure 9J) similar to conventionalized animals (Figure 8A,B and I).
evidence: This is supported by monoassociation experiments and morphology quantification shown in Figure 9J.

claim: Monoassociation with Acinetobacter sp. ZOR0008 alone is sufficient to reduce EEC calcium response to palmitate stimulation following high fat feeding compared with germ-free controls.
source: Consistently, we also found that monoassociation with Acinetobacter sp. ZOR0008 alone is sufficient to reduce EEC calcium response to palmitate stimulation following HF feeding compared with GF controls (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment with NAC or L-NAME does not prevent high fat feeding induced EEC silencing in zebrafish.
source: We first treated conventional raised zebrafish with known ROS scavengers N-acetylcysteine (NAC) (Mocelin et al., 2019) and N(ω)-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME) that can inhibit host reactive nitrogen species production (Bradley et al., 2010), however neither of these compounds prevented HF feeding induced EEC silencing (Figure 9—figure supplement 3A–D and G).
evidence: This is supported by morphology quantification data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3A–D and G.

claim: There are no significant differences in intestinal fluorescence in the conditions of germ-free, conventionalized, and Acinetobacter sp. monoassociated zebrafish with or without high fat feeding using CM-H2DCFDA.
source: Using a general oxidative stress chemical indicator CM-H2DCFDA whose fluorescence can be induced by ROS mediated oxidation, we also failed to detect significant differences in intestinal fluoresence in the conditions of GF, CV and Acinetobacter sp. monoassociated zebrafish with or without HF feeding (Figure 9—figure supplement 3E–F and H).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3E–F and H.

claim: There is no significant induction of ROS production in in vitro cultures of Aeromonas sp. and Acinetobacter sp. in media containing high fat meal.
source: Similarly we did not observe significant induction of ROS production in in vitro cultures of Aeromonas sp. and Acinetobacter sp. in media containing HF meal (Figure 9—figure supplement 3I).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ROS measurement data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3I.

claim: The development and physiology of the zebrafish digestive tract are similar to those of mammals.
source: The development and physiology of the zebrafish digestive tract are similar to those of mammals (Wallace et al., 2005; Wallace and Pack, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Zebrafish hatch from their protective chorions at 3 days post-fertilization (dpf).
source: Zebrafish hatch from their protective chorions at 3 days post-fertilization (dpf) and microbial colonization of the intestinal lumen begins shortly thereafter (Rawls et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish development supported by a citation.

claim: Microbial colonization of the zebrafish intestinal lumen begins shortly after hatching at 3 dpf.
source: Zebrafish hatch from their protective chorions at 3 days post-fertilization (dpf) and microbial colonization of the intestinal lumen begins shortly thereafter (Rawls et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The zebrafish intestine becomes completely patent by 4 dpf.
source: The zebrafish intestine becomes completely patent by 4 dpf and feeding and digestion begin around 5 dpf.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish development.

claim: Feeding and digestion begin around 5 dpf in zebrafish.
source: The zebrafish intestine becomes completely patent by 4 dpf and feeding and digestion begin around 5 dpf.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish development.

claim: The zebrafish intestine develops most of the same differentiated epithelial cell types as observed in mammals, including absorptive enterocytes, mucus-secreting goblet cells, and EECs.
source: The zebrafish intestine develops most of the same differentiated epithelial cell types as observed in mammals, including absorptive enterocytes, mucus-secreting goblet cells, and EECs (Ng et al., 2005; Wallace et al., 2005; Wallace and Pack, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Absorption of dietary fat occurs primarily in enterocytes within the proximal intestine of the zebrafish.
source: Absorption of dietary fat occur primarily in enterocytes within the proximal intestine of the zebrafish (Quinlivan and Farber, 2017) (yellow area in Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and indicated in Figure 1D.

claim: The conserved aspects of intestinal epithelial anatomy and physiology in zebrafish are associated with a conserved transcriptional regulatory program shared between zebrafish and mammals.
source: These conserved aspects of intestinal epithelial anatomy and physiology are associated with a conserved transcriptional regulatory program shared between zebrafish and mammals (Lickwar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The zebrafish intestine is colonized by a complex microbiota which promotes intestinal absorption of dietary fat.
source: The zebrafish intestine is colonized by a complex microbiota which promotes intestinal absorption of dietary fat (Semova et al., 2012) but microbial and nutritional effects on zebrafish EEC physiology were unknown.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Consumption of dietary fat contributes to metabolic disorders.
source: Consumption of dietary fat contributes to metabolic disorders, but EEC adaptations to high fat feeding were unknown.
evidence: This is general knowledge about the relationship between dietary fat and metabolic health.

claim: EECs synthesize and secrete hormones in response to ingested nutrients including carbohydrates, fatty acids, peptides and amino acids.
source: EECs synthesize and secrete hormones in response to ingested nutrients including carbohydrates, fatty acids, peptides and amino acids (Delzenne et al., 2007; Moran-Ramos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nutrients directly stimulate EECs by triggering a cascade of membrane depolarization, action potential firing and voltage dependent calcium entry.
source: These nutrients directly stimulate EECs by triggering a cascade of membrane depolarization, action potential firing and voltage dependent calcium entry.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EEC physiology.

claim: Increase of intracellular calcium can trigger the fusion of hormone-containing vesicles with the cytoplasmic membrane and hormone release in EECs.
source: Increase of intracellular calcium ([Ca2+]i) can trigger the fusion of hormone-containing vesicles with the cytoplasmic membrane and hormone release (Sternini et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The apical surfaces of most EECs are exposed to the gut lumen allowing them to detect ingested luminal contents.
source: The apical surfaces of most EECs are exposed to the gut lumen allowing them to detect ingested luminal contents (Gribble and Reimann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Some EECs are not open to the gut lumen and reside close to the basal lamina.
source: However, some EECs are not open to the gut lumen and reside close to the basal lamina (Höfer et al., 1999; Sternini et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Different morphological types of EECs are classified as 'open' or 'closed' EECs respectively.
source: These different morphological types are classified as 'open' or 'closed' EECs respectively, and traditionally have been thought to reflect distinct developmental cell fates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EEC classification.

claim: More than 15 different hormones have been identified in EECs.
source: More than 15 different hormones have been identified in EECs which exert broad physiological effects on gut motility, satiation, food digestion, nutrient absorption, insulin sensitivity, and energy storage (Moran-Ramos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: EEC hormones exert broad physiological effects on gut motility, satiation, food digestion, nutrient absorption, insulin sensitivity, and energy storage.
source: More than 15 different hormones have been identified in EECs which exert broad physiological effects on gut motility, satiation, food digestion, nutrient absorption, insulin sensitivity, and energy storage (Moran-Ramos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: EECs communicate through circulating hormones and through direct paracrine and neuronal signaling to multiple systems including the intrinsic and extrinsic nervous system, pancreas, liver and adipose tissue.
source: EECs communicate not only through circulating hormones, but also through direct paracrine and neuronal signaling to multiple systems including the intrinsic and extrinsic nervous system, pancreas, liver and adipose tissue (Bohórquez et al., 2015; Gribble and Reimann, 2016; Kaelberer et al., 2018; Latorre et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EECs have a key role in regulating energy homeostasis and represent the first link that connects dietary nutrient status to systemic metabolic processes.
source: EECs therefore have a key role in regulating energy homeostasis and represent the first link that connects dietary nutrient status to systemic metabolic processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the established functions of EECs.

claim: The percentage of energy intake from fat remains approximately 33% in the US.
source: Despite efforts to reduce dietary fat intake in recent decades, the percentage of energy intake from fat remains ~33% in the US (Austin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: High levels of dietary fat have a dominant effect on energy intake and adiposity.
source: High levels of dietary fat have a dominant effect on energy intake and adiposity (Zhao et al., 2018) and have been implicated in the high prevalence of human metabolic disorders worldwide (Ludwig et al., 2018; Oakes et al., 1997; Panchal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: High levels of dietary fat have been implicated in the high prevalence of human metabolic disorders worldwide.
source: High levels of dietary fat have a dominant effect on energy intake and adiposity (Zhao et al., 2018) and have been implicated in the high prevalence of human metabolic disorders worldwide (Ludwig et al., 2018; Oakes et al., 1997; Panchal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Consumption of a high fat diet affects the microbial communities residing in the intestine.
source: It is also well appreciated that consumption of a high fat diet affects the microbial communities residing in the intestine, commonly refered to as the gut microbiota (David et al., 2014; Hildebrandt et al., 2009; Murphy et al., 2010; Turnbaugh et al., 2008; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gut microbiota altered by high fat diet can promote adiposity and insulin resistance.
source: Gnotobiotic animal studies also demonstrated that gut microbiota altered by high fat diet can promote adiposity and insulin resistance (Ridaura et al., 2013; Turnbaugh et al., 2008; Turnbaugh et al., 2006), but the underlying mechanisms are incompletely understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous gnotobiotic studies.

claim: Many gastrointestinal hormones have very short half-lives.
source: However, many gastrointestinal hormones have very short half-lives and peripheral plasma hormone levels do not mirror real-time EEC function (Cuenco et al., 2017; Druce et al., 2009; Kieffer et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Peripheral plasma hormone levels do not mirror real-time EEC function.
source: However, many gastrointestinal hormones have very short half-lives and peripheral plasma hormone levels do not mirror real-time EEC function (Cuenco et al., 2017; Druce et al., 2009; Kieffer et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In vitro culture systems are unable to mimic the dynamic and complex luminal environment that contains food and microbiota.
source: Moreover, in vitro culture systems are unable to mimic the dynamic and complex luminal environment that contains food and microbiota.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of in vitro systems.

claim: High fat feeding in mice reduces intestinal glucose sensing and glucose induced GLP-1 secretion in vivo.
source: The observation that EECs exhibited reduced sensitivity to oral glucose following high fat feeding is interesting and consistent with the finding in mice that high fat feeding reduces intestinal glucose sensing and glucose induced GLP-1 secretion in vivo (Bauer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous mouse study.

claim: Small intestinal cultures from high fat fed mice exhibit reduced secretory responsiveness to nutrient stimuli including glucose when compared with cultures from control mice.
source: In vitro, small intestinal cultures from high fat fed mice also exhibit reduced secretory responsiveness to nutrient stimuli including glucose when compared with cultures from control mice (Richards et al., 2016) but underlying mechanisms remained unclear.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous in vitro study.

claim: Gut microbiota promote intestinal absorption of dietary fat in zebrafish.
source: Using the same HF feeding model in zebrafish, we previously showed that the gut microbiota promote intestinal absorption and metabolism of dietary fatty acids (Semova et al., 2012), and similar roles for microbiota have been established recently in mouse (Martinez-Guryn et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous zebrafish study.

claim: Gut microbiota promote intestinal absorption and metabolism of dietary fatty acids in mice.
source: Using the same HF feeding model in zebrafish, we previously showed that the gut microbiota promote intestinal absorption and metabolism of dietary fatty acids (Semova et al., 2012), and similar roles for microbiota have been established recently in mouse (Martinez-Guryn et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent mouse study.

claim: Lipid digestion and absorption is impaired in germ-free animals.
source: Previous studies in gnotobiotic zebrafish and mice have shown that lipid digestion and absorption is impaired in germ-free animals and enterocytes in germ-free conditions exhibit reduced lipid droplet accumulation (Martinez-Guryn et al., 2018; Semova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous gnotobiotic studies.

claim: Enterocytes in germ-free conditions exhibit reduced lipid droplet accumulation.
source: Previous studies in gnotobiotic zebrafish and mice have shown that lipid digestion and absorption is impaired in germ-free animals and enterocytes in germ-free conditions exhibit reduced lipid droplet accumulation (Martinez-Guryn et al., 2018; Semova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous gnotobiotic studies.

claim: Acinetobacter was enriched in adult zebrafish gut following a chronic high fat diet.
source: Acinetobacter was the most highly enriched genus in the larval zebrafish intestine following high fat feeding in this study and was also enriched in adult zebrafish gut following a chronic high fat diet (Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A. baumannii can signal to host epithelial cells through secreted outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) and activation of downstream inflammatory pathways.
source: Studies suggest that A. baumannii, a related oportunitistic pathogen, can signal to host epithelial cells through secreted outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) and activation of downstream inflammatory pathways (Jha et al., 2017; Jin et al., 2011; Jun et al., 2013; March et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on A. baumannii.

claim: Acinetobacter strains are known to secrete phospholipase that can affect host cell membrane stability and interfere with host signaling.
source: In addition to OMVs, Acinetobacter strains are known to secrete phospholipase that can affect host cell membrane stability and interfere with host signaling (Lee et al., 2017; Songer, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Members of the Acinetobacter genus are known to possess potent oil degrading and lipolytic activities.
source: Members of the Acinetobacter genus are also known to possess potent oil degrading and lipolytic activities (Lal and Khanna, 1996; Snellman and Colwell, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Species from Acinetobacter genus have the ability to produce emulsifiers which might enhance lipid digestion.
source: Moreover, species from Acinetobacter genus have the ability to produce emulsifiers which might enhance lipid digestion (Navon-Venezia et al., 1995; Toren et al., 2001; Walzer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acinetobacter spp. in the human gut are positively associated with plasma triglycerides and total- and LDL-cholesterol.
source: Acinetobacter spp. in the human gut are positively associated with plasma triglycerides and total- and LDL-cholesterol (Graessler et al., 2013), and Acinetobacter spp. are also enriched in the crypts of the small intestine and colon in mammals (Mao et al., 2015; Pédron et al., 2012; Saffarian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human and mammalian studies.

claim: Acinetobacter spp. are enriched in the crypts of the small intestine and colon in mammals.
source: Acinetobacter spp. in the human gut are positively associated with plasma triglycerides and total- and LDL-cholesterol (Graessler et al., 2013), and Acinetobacter spp. are also enriched in the crypts of the small intestine and colon in mammals (Mao et al., 2015; Pédron et al., 2012; Saffarian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mammalian studies.
